Wanderlust — Travel Platform
Concept, product design and interface system for a modern trip discovery & booking experience.

Discovery is broken
before booking even starts

01 — PROBLEM
01

Filters before feeling

Search-first tools ask travelers to already know what they want — destination, dates, budget — before showing them anything worth wanting.

02

Booking reads like a form

Dense fields, seat maps and fine print arrive before any emotional reason to book. The product feels like admin work, not a trip.

03

The trip disappears after checkout

Most tools stop caring the moment payment clears. Documents, rewards and flight status scatter across emails and other apps.

Wanderlust starts from a different assumption: inspiration and logistics can share one screen — the trip should feel real from the very first search, not just after it's paid for.

About the
project

02 — ABOUT

The idea

Most travel sites sell logistics — dates, prices, seat maps — before they sell the feeling of a place. Wanderlust flips the order: destinations lead with mood and imagery, and the transactional parts of booking sit quietly underneath, ready when the traveler is.

The problem

Search-first travel tools ask people to know exactly what they want before showing them anything worth wanting. Filters come before inspiration, forms come before feeling — efficient for a returning customer, cold for everyone else.

The solution

A discovery layer that reads like an editorial magazine, paired with a booking flow dense enough for a frequent flyer and calm enough for a first-timer. One dashboard ties every trip, document and reward together after booking.

04 — FLOW

Four surfaces, one line of thought: a traveler moves from an open-ended mood to a held itinerary without ever feeling like they switched products.

Design decision

Booking (04) is deliberately the narrowest step, not the biggest — every other surface is built to make this one boring and fast, because the emotional work already happened upstream.

✦ SCREEN 01 — LANDING

The first screen sets the mood

A full-bleed split hero pairs an emotional headline with a glass search panel — the traveler can dream and plan in the same glance, without picking one or the other first.

✦ SCREEN 02 — DISCOVERY, ANNOTATED

Search that feels like inspiration

Mood tags sit above filters, personalized picks sit above the fold — the page leads with "what if" before it asks "how much."

1 2 3 4 5
1

Global search

Destinations, hotels and experiences in one field — no mode switching before typing.

2

Emotional headline

Time-of-day greeting plus an open question, not a form label.

3

Time-boxed deal

Countdown and struck-through price create gentle urgency without a popup.

4

Quick actions

Flexible dates, inspiration and worry-free travel — answers to hesitation, not features.

5

Mood-first filters

"Beaches", "Culture", "Romantic" — a feeling to tap, before any date or budget field.

Who this is
designed for

05 — PERSONA

No user research backs this — it's the working assumption that shaped every trade-off above. Written down so the decisions can be argued with.

EM

The improviser

Books 3-4 leisure trips a year, mid-planning
"I don't know exactly where yet — show me something, then let me get serious fast."
Wants
  • Inspiration before commitment
  • A price she can trust at a glance
  • One place to hold the whole trip after booking
Maps to
  • Mood-first discovery (Problem 01)
  • Pinned, single-button booking (Problem 02)
  • The personal travel hub (Problem 03)
✦ SCREEN 03 — DESTINATION

The heaviest information page in the product — facts, gallery, itinerary, reviews — stays legible because the booking card is pinned and self-contained.

Impact

The redesign wasn't meant to add more steps. It was built to help travelers feel ready before they even book.

Rather than counting clicks, success is measured by how much uncertainty disappears between opening the app and holding a confirmed trip.

Format

08 — PLATFORM

Wanderlust is designed desktop-first, as a planning surface: wide layouts, side-by-side comparison, room for a persistent sidebar and a floating booking summary.

Mobile and tablet adaptations are the next milestone — the component system was built with enough restraint that it should compress cleanly into a single column without a redesign.
